t: Abolitionism grew from Quaker and evangelical protest into the first great campaigns of petitions, boycotts and public testimony, aimed first at the Atlantic slave trade and then at slavery itself.
Enslaved people fought for their own freedom throughout: the Haitian Revolution, great revolts in the British Caribbean and countless escapes pushed governments towards abolition.
By the time of Brazil’s Golden Law in 1888 slavery had been abolished throughout the Americas, but freedom rarely brought the formerly enslaved land, compensation or equality.
dyk: Brazil’s Golden Law of 13 May 1888, which ended slavery in the last country of the Americas to keep it, has just two articles: the first declares slavery extinct in Brazil, the second revokes all provisions to the contrary.
ev: Quakers and Anglicans found the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade in London
Enslaved people rise in Saint-Domingue; their revolution ends slavery there and founds Haiti in 1804
Britain and the United States ban the Atlantic slave trade
Samuel Sharpe’s rising begins in Jamaica; in Boston William Lloyd Garrison founds The Liberator
The Slavery Abolition Act frees the enslaved across most of the British Empire from 1834
France and Denmark abolish slavery in their colonies
The Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery throughout the United States
Princess Isabel signs Brazil’s Golden Law, ending slavery in the last country of the Americas to keep it

f.where: Arose among Quakers and evangelical Christians in Britain and North America; spread to France, the Caribbean, Spanish America and Brazil, and drew strength from the resistance of the enslaved
f.period: 1787–1888: from the founding of the London committee against the slave trade to Brazil’s Golden Law; Quaker protests reach back to 1688, and campaigns against slavery in Africa and Asia went on into the 20th century
f.figures: Thomas Clarkson, Olaudah Equiano, William Wilberforce, Toussaint Louverture, Frederick Douglass, Joaquim Nabuco
f.outcome: The Atlantic slave trade was outlawed and suppressed and slavery abolished throughout the Americas by 1888; owners were often compensated, while the freed rarely received land or equal rights
